post.description:
The first call a client makes, and the one every later call is planned against.

Nothing here depends on who is asking: the answer describes the portal, not the caller, and
the method reads nothing the caller owns. What it publishes is the schema version, the
vocabulary of entities and of changes, the page ceilings, how long the journal of changes
keeps a record, how long an interaction keeps an object in sight, and the three polling
steps - the shortest one allowed, the recommended one and the longest one still accepted.

`interactionWindowDays` is the one number that is about the memory of the portal rather than
about the journal. An object a user only ever touched - opened through a link, or reached
through an attachment of another module - is theirs to see while the window lasts, and is
announced as a tombstone once it runs out. Nothing happened to such an object; the portal
stopped counting the interaction as a reason to show it.

The numbers are not constants of the product. A portal may shorten the life of its journal,
and the polling bounds move with it, so a client that stores them once and never asks again
will eventually plan against bounds the portal no longer honours. Ask on every start of a
synchronisation cycle.

`cardSections` names every section the schema declares and says, for each, whether this
portal fills it. A section published as `false` is refused when it is asked for rather than
answered empty: an empty section would be indistinguishable from "nothing is there".

`publicLinkPolicy` says whether the portal opens manual external links at the moment -
`manualLinks` - and manual links to boards - `boardLinks`, which follows `manualLinks` while
boards are off on the portal. The `publicAccess` of a card describes the link itself and not
this policy, and the client applies the policy on its own: `boardLinks` to a direct link on
a board, `manualLinks` to every other source, folders included. A change of the policy gives
no record in the journal; the client learns of it by asking this method again.

post.summary: One page of the journal of changes
post.description:
Hands over what has happened to the files of the caller since the position they name, in the
order the portal published it.

Ask for the next page with the `nextCursor` of the previous one and stop when `hasMore` says
the journal is over. A page that came back short is not the end of it: records fall out to
the confirmation of visibility, and only `hasMore` answers that question. `hasMore` is
decided against the tail the portal considers settled, so the youngest records of the
journal - the ones that may still be on their way in - are held back rather than handed over
and forgotten. That is what disk.sync.capabilities.get publishes as safeWindowSeconds, and
it is applied by the server: a client neither names that boundary nor has to compensate for
it.

Applying the same page twice is safe. The cursor moves only over records the page actually
walked, so a client that failed before it saved the cursor asks with the old one and is
handed the same records again - and applying a change of an object, a tombstone or a change
of access a second time leaves the memory of the client exactly as the first time did.

A record about an object carries the card of that object as it stood when the record was
published. A tombstone and a change of access carry no card at all, which is what lets them
reach a client that can no longer see the object: a tombstone says what the client holds is
to be dropped, a change of access says a boundary of visibility moved and names the scope to
look at again.

A record about a folder stands for everything under it. A move, a trashing, a restoring and
the deletion of a folder go down its whole subtree and give one record, on the folder: the
objects under it are given no records of their own, and what follows for them the client
works out on its own tree. A place lies under the folder when the folder is among
`places[].path` or is `places[].parentFolderId` - on the tree as it stands now, not on paths
kept from before a folder above was moved. A tombstone of a folder takes away, with all of
its places and without a request, every object that had a place under it reached through
folders alone (`reachedByLink` false). A place under it reached through a link of the
reader is dropped and the object is asked about by disk.sync.state.check: it may be a folder
of someone else whose link lay inside the deleted one, and that folder lives on. The objects
with no place or with a cut path are asked about the same way. A trashing and a restoring of
a folder change `trashed` and `trashedWithAncestor` of the places under it with no record of
their own: a trashing marks every such place as trashed with an ancestor, those already in
the trash on their own included; a restoring clears both, except on an object that stays in
the trash on its own - `trashed` true, `trashedWithAncestor` false - and under it. The
tombstone of a folder goes to the readers of the folder. Whoever held a file under it by an
interaction alone gets a tombstone of that file; whoever saw an object under it by an access
of their own and does not read the folder may get no record at all, and learns of it by
disk.sync.state.check.

`cursor` belongs to the pair of a user and an application, and not to the user alone. A
cursor handed to another application of the same user is refused with CURSOR_INVALID, the
same code as a cursor of another user or a damaged one. The cursor outlives the session it
came with: opening a session again does not annul it, and a client that has just replaced
its session goes on reading the journal from where it stood.

`cursorExpiresAt` is when the position stops being accepted. It is stamped when the session
was created and is not moved by reading: the position handed out by the newest page carries
the same moment as the one the session began with. A session is therefore read for the
retention of the journal counted from its creation - disk.sync.capabilities.get publishes
that as journalRetentionDays - however fresh the position of the client is, and after that
every position of that session is refused with CURSOR_EXPIRED.

A client that means to go on reading creates a session again before that moment. The cheap
way is to do it while caught up: read until `hasMore` says the journal is over, create the
session straight away and go on from the cursor it hands back. In that order nothing is
lost and nothing has to be reconciled - the cursor of a new session is stamped a safe
window back from the moment it was created, so a client that has just reached the end of
the journal is handed a position at or behind its own, and the records it is handed twice
change nothing. The fetch token of that session may simply be left unused: this is not a
reason to run the initial fetch again.

Rebuilding the memory is the answer to a position that was already refused, and only to
that. A client that let its cursor expire cannot learn what happened while it was away -
the journal no longer holds those records - so it reads the initial fetch of a new session
and asks disk.sync.state.check about everything it still holds that the fetch did not name.

`warnings` names what the page could not describe, and `reason` says which of the two it
was. OBJECT_UNAVAILABLE is an object that is still visible to the caller and has no card to
build - it was deleted between the publication of the record and the assembly of the page.
RECORD_UNREADABLE is a record whose own shape is outside this contract: a kind of resource,
a kind of change or a reason for a tombstone the server does not know, which is what a
portal being deployed node by node produces while the rollout lasts. In both cases the page
is formed round such a record and the position moves past it, so one unreadable object
cannot stop the journal of a client for good. The identifier is part of the warning, because
that is what lets a client read the object back - by disk.sync.state.check, which is the
only way a warned record is ever recovered: the journal does not offer it again.

Six types report a change of the sharing or of the public access of an object:
sharingCreated, sharingUpdated and sharingDeleted, publicAccessEnabled, publicAccessUpdated
and publicAccessDisabled. Each is an ordinary update with the card of the object and one
more field, `affectsDescendants`: true on a folder, whose one record stands for everything
under it, and false on a file. The objects under a folder are not given records of their
own. The type names the operation - over the explicit rights of the object, or over its own
manual external link - and not the state it led to; the state is read from the card. So
a lifetime moved into the past, or given back to a link that had run out, is
publicAccessUpdated although the object stops or starts being public, and the deletion of
the own link of an object inside a public folder is publicAccessDisabled while the card
says the object is still public by inheritance. The card carries `access` only when the
request asked for it; a client that did not ask learns the state with disk.sync.state.check
and that section.

One operation may give such a record and a change of access together. The change of access
goes to those whose visibility may have moved and sends them to reconcile; the record with
the card goes to the readers of the object and is applied. The order of the two is not
guaranteed. The record of a sharing is addressed to the readers of the object before the
edit: a new recipient learns of the object from the change of access and the reconciliation
after it, and a user the object was taken from gets the change of access alone. A change on
a folder the caller does not read reaches nobody who reads only an object under it.

The `access` section says who else the object is open to. It is filled only when the
request names it in `sections`: a request without `sections` goes without it. `canRead` is
always true: the object has already passed the check of visibility. `canDownload` is present
on a file only and equals the `contentAvailable` of the same card. `internalSharing.enabled` says that the object itself
carries explicit rights beyond the base rights of its storage, `internalSharing.inherited`
that a folder above it, below the root of the storage, carries them, and `targets` names the
recipients of the rights of the object itself as pairs of `type` and `id`: user, workgroup,
department and chat carry an id; allUsers (every authorised user), everyone (unauthorised
visitors included) and other carry none. `publicAccess.enabled` says that the object is
public by a manual external link that is still alive; while it is, the section names one
source - `effectiveSource` direct or inherited, `inheritedFromFolderId`, `permission` view
or edit, `expiresAt` and `passwordProtected` - and `hasOtherSources` says that more than one
link makes the object public. A link on the object itself comes before the links on its
versions, and those before the nearest public folder above.

What the section shows is never wider than the access interface of Disk shows the caller,
and it is shown whole or not at all. The flags - `internalSharing.enabled`,
`internalSharing.inherited`, `publicAccess.enabled`, `effectiveSource` and
`hasOtherSources` - reach every reader of the object. `targets` reaches a caller who may
change the rights of the object, and a caller who may only share it when every target comes
from sharing; an absent `targets` means "not shown", an empty array means "nobody". The
source folder and the parameters of an inherited link are shown when the caller reads that
folder and every folder between it and the object; a source above a folder the caller does
not read is told only as the fact of inherited public access. `expiresAt: null` means the
link never expires, an absent `expiresAt` means the parameters are not shown. Whether the
portal opens manual links at the moment is not a part of the section: it is
`publicLinkPolicy` of disk.sync.capabilities.get, and the client applies it itself.

post.summary: Where to fetch the bytes of a file
post.description:
Turns the download identifier of a card into a link to the content of that file.

The method answers with a link and never with bytes: `url` is fetched with an ordinary GET
and needs no header, no session and no scope beyond the one this call was already made
with. `expiresAt` says when the link stops being accepted; ask for a new one rather than
storing this one. A link is cheap to ask for again, and asking again is what re-checks the
rights - so a client planning a long queue of downloads should ask shortly before it
fetches rather than collect links in advance.

The rights of the caller are checked twice: once here, and once more when the link is
presented. A right taken away in between is a refused download, not an open one.

ACCESS_DENIED is the single answer to everything an identifier can be wrong about - a file
the caller does not see, a file whose content this portal calls unavailable, an identifier
of a kind the portal does not serve, an identifier that was never issued at all. They are
one answer on purpose: the identifier is opaque, and telling those cases apart would let
the objects of a portal be probed through the refusals.

OBJECT_NOT_FOUND says something narrower and is never a way to learn whether an object
exists: it is answered only for an object the caller does see and whose content is gone
from the portal.

historyDepthDays.description: How far back the history of files is asked for, in days. The portal may serve less than was asked for and says how much in effectiveHistoryDepthDays, so a depth above what it serves is not an error.

plannedPollIntervalSeconds.description: How often the client intends to come back for changes, in seconds. Checked against the bounds disk.sync.capabilities.get publishes and then only recorded - nothing on the server is timed by it. A value outside the bounds is refused rather than trimmed.

post.description:
Fixes everything the initial fetch is read against and hands back the two positions the
client works from.

A session belongs to a pair - the user and the application calling on their behalf - and
not to the user alone. Two applications of the same user hold two independent sessions and
cannot use each other's positions.

`snapshotToken` is the position of the initial fetch and stops being accepted at
`snapshotTokenExpiresAt`; a fetch that did not finish by then is started again with a new
session rather than stitched onto the old one. `cursor` is the position in the journal of
changes. It is handed out together with the session because the two are read in turn from
the very beginning: what the fetch has not reached, the journal already keeps. The cursor
outlives the session it came with - it belongs to the pair, and creating a session again
does not annul it - but it does not outlive the retention of the journal counted from that
creation, and creating a session again does not extend it either. Every position of one
session stops being accepted at the same moment, however far it has been read.

Creating a session again while one is live is a normal thing to do, and a client changing
its polling step does exactly that. The previous session is replaced and its fetch token
stops matching; the cursor of the previous session keeps working, so a change of session is
not a re-read of the journal. A client that means to go on reading for longer than the
retention of the journal has to do this before the cursor of its current session expires -
disk.sync.changes.list says when that is and how it is done without reconciling anything.

`effectiveHistoryDepthDays` is always answered, including when it equals what was asked for:
a client handed less than it asked for without being told would take the shorter answer for
the whole of its history.

`approximateObjectCount` and `approximateObjectCountComplete` are a lower bound of what the
initial fetch is about to deliver and whether that bound is the whole of it. Both are absent
from the answer - not null - when no storage of the user could be counted without checking
rights per object: a client has to be able to tell "the portal cannot estimate this cheaply"
from "there is nothing", and a zero would say the second.

post.summary: One page of the initial fetch
post.description:
Hands over the personal copy of a client page by page, in the order the client needs it
rather than in the order the portal stores it.

The page is read against the state the session fixed, so a page is repeatable: an object
that changes while the fetch is running neither moves between pages nor falls out of it.
Ask for the next page with the `nextSnapshotToken` of the previous one, and stop when

rows are lost to the collapsing of links and to the confirmation of the interaction set,
and only `hasMore` says whether anything is left.

`folders` is a section of its own and is not counted into `limit`. Folders join the fetch
by kinship - as the readable folders above the objects of the page - and not by their own
freshness: the date a folder changed says nothing about the activity inside it, and a
folder untouched for years may well hold the files a client asked for. Folders are
deduplicated inside a page; a folder met again on a later page is normal and costs the
client nothing, because applying the card of a folder is idempotent.

Every folder a path of the page names has a card in `folders`. A folder of somebody else
that the caller reaches through a link of their own enters the path as that link, under
the link's own name, and the card of that link is answered beside the ancestors. The one
identifier that may be answered without a card is `parentFolderId` of a place whose path
does not reach it: the folder then lies above the boundary of access, and no name of it is
published anywhere.

`snapshotToken` stops being accepted at the `snapshotTokenExpiresAt` of its session, and a
fetch that did not finish by then is started again with a new session rather than stitched
onto the old one. The same refusal answers a token of a session that has since been
replaced - opening a session again annuls the fetch of the previous one.

`warnings` names what the page could not deliver: an object deleted between the fetch that
named it and the assembly that describes it arrives as a warning rather than as a card.
The identifier is part of it, because that is what lets a client read the object back
instead of discovering the gap by comparing counts.

The `access` section says who else the object is open to. It is filled only when the
request names it in `sections`: a request without `sections` goes without it. `canRead` is
always true: the object has already passed the check of visibility. `canDownload` is present

or edit, `expiresAt` and `passwordProtected` - and `hasOtherSources` says that more than one
link makes the object public. A link on the object itself comes before the links on its
versions, and those before the nearest public folder above.

What the section shows is never wider than the access interface of Disk shows the caller,
and it is shown whole or not at all. The flags - `internalSharing.enabled`,
`internalSharing.inherited`, `publicAccess.enabled`, `effectiveSource` and
`hasOtherSources` - reach every reader of the object. `targets` reaches a caller who may
change the rights of the object, and a caller who may only share it when every target comes
from sharing; an absent `targets` means "not shown", an empty array means "nobody". The
source folder and the parameters of an inherited link are shown when the caller reads that

Answers what the journal cannot: what a client still sees, after a position it can no
longer read from and after a boundary of visibility moved.

The method has two modes and the request chooses between them by what it carries. Name
`objectIds` to ask about the objects the memory of the client already holds. Name
`scopeRootId` to ask about an area - the root a change of access named. A request that
names both is refused, and so is one that names neither: guessing which was meant would
answer a question that was not asked.

Over a list the answer holds exactly one item per object, in the order the objects were
asked about. Over an area the answer is a page: ask for the next one with the
`nextCheckToken` of the previous, and stop when `hasMore` says the area is over. A page
that came back short is not the end of it - links inside an area collapse onto the object
they point at - and only `hasMore` answers that question.

An object the caller does not see is answered `visible: false` and carries no card. That
answer is the same for an object hidden from the caller and for an object that was never
there: the method never asks whether an object exists, so it cannot be used to find out.
For the same reason an area whose root the caller cannot see is answered with an empty
finished page rather than with a refusal - which is the ordinary case, not an edge one:
the first move of a reconciliation runs right after a revocation, when the root is already
invisible.

An area whose root is perfectly visible answers the same way when everything in it changed
too recently, and a client that reads an empty finished page as an empty area loses those
objects for good. A page is read against a boundary of state standing a little behind the
current instant, and what changed above that boundary enters no page of the walk. So an
empty finished first move does not mean an empty area: repeat the first move on the next
step of polling before treating the area as walked through. `safeWindowSeconds` is not that
boundary - it describes the journal and the initial fetch, while a walk over an area is read
against a narrower one of its own.

A visible object may arrive without a card. It was deleted between the verdict that named
it and the assembly that describes it; the client reads it back and waits for the journal
to say otherwise, rather than dropping an object it has just been told it can see.

The check answers about the state of right now. No depth of history is applied to it -
bounded by depth it would say "you do not see it" about a visible object that simply had
not changed for a long time - and objects in the trashcan are visible objects like any
other. The consequence is accepted: after a check the memory of a client may hold objects
older than the depth its session was given.

The check moves no cursor, reads no journal and neither needs a session nor touches one.
`checkToken` is its own kind of position with a boundary of state and a life of its own,
and an expired one is refused with CHECK_TOKEN_EXPIRED - a code of its own, so that a
client does not go and recreate a session the check never used. A token of another user,
of another application of the same user, of another kind or damaged in any way is refused
with CURSOR_INVALID.

The `access` section says who else the object is open to. It is filled only when the
request names it in `sections`: a request without `sections` goes without it. `canRead` is
always true: the object has already passed the check of visibility. `canDownload` is present
on a file only and equals the `contentAvailable` of the same card. `internalSharing.enabled` says that the object itself
carries explicit rights beyond the base rights of its storage, `internalSharing.inherited`
that a folder above it, below the root of the storage, carries them, and `targets` names the
recipients of the rights of the object itself as pairs of `type` and `id`: user, workgroup,
department and chat carry an id; allUsers (every authorised user), everyone (unauthorised
visitors included) and other carry none. `publicAccess.enabled` says that the object is
public by a manual external link that is still alive; while it is, the section names one
source - `effectiveSource` direct or inherited, `inheritedFromFolderId`, `permission` view
or edit, `expiresAt` and `passwordProtected` - and `hasOtherSources` says that more than one
link makes the object public. A link on the object itself comes before the links on its
versions, and those before the nearest public folder above.

What the section shows is never wider than the access interface of Disk shows the caller,
and it is shown whole or not at all. The flags - `internalSharing.enabled`,
`internalSharing.inherited`, `publicAccess.enabled`, `effectiveSource` and
`hasOtherSources` - reach every reader of the object. `targets` reaches a caller who may
change the rights of the object, and a caller who may only share it when every target comes
from sharing; an absent `targets` means "not shown", an empty array means "nobody". The
source folder and the parameters of an inherited link are shown when the caller reads that
folder and every folder between it and the object; a source above a folder the caller does
not read is told only as the fact of inherited public access. `expiresAt: null` means the
link never expires, an absent `expiresAt` means the parameters are not shown. Whether the
portal opens manual links at the moment is not a part of the section: it is
`publicLinkPolicy` of disk.sync.capabilities.get, and the client applies it itself.

objectId.description: The identifier of the board file from its synchronisation card.

validation.description: Present when the request itself was refused. One entry per parameter.

post.summary: Get the prepared index of a board
post.description:
Returns the current prepared index of a board as UTF-8 text.

The method checks the user and application pair, current access to the object, the file type
and the state of the prepared index on every call. A card that says the index is available is
not an access grant.

BOARD_INDEX_NOT_FOUND is the single answer for an absent object, a non-file, a file that is
not a board and an object the caller cannot currently read. These cases are deliberately
indistinguishable, so the method cannot be used to probe objects outside the caller's access.

BOARD_INDEX_NOT_READY means the board is readable but has no prepared index yet. The same
answer is used while indexing is waiting and after an indexing attempt failed. Keep the
previously downloaded index and wait for the next indexUpdated change.

A ready empty board is successful and returns an empty `text`. The response contains no object
identifier, storage fields or index version.

Starts the generation of a site from the description and answers with the state of the started generation - the same state landing.aisite.status is then asked about, so a start the limits already refused is read from this answer instead of from a second call. The description is required and holds at most 4000 characters. Sending the same request twice is only protected against when the client sends an `Idempotency-Key` header, and only once the first call has answered: the answer reaches the store when the call ends, and a repeat with the same key then gives it back instead of starting a second generation - the key is remembered for 24 hours. A repeat sent while the first call is still running is not covered by the key: while the site draft is still free it is refused as a competing call, and once the first call has taken the draft it starts a second generation of its own. A client that gives up on the answer by a timeout and repeats the start therefore risks a second generation. Without the header every call starts a new generation. The generation takes the one free site draft the user has, the same draft the AI site chat of the portal works on: a chat the user has open at that moment loses its draft and has to be reloaded, so do not start a generation for a user who is working in the chat.

post.summary: State of an AI site generation
post.description: Reads the state of a generation: `running` while it is going, `completed` with the identifiers of the created site and page, or `failed` with the reason. A generation of another user is answered as a missing one, so that its existence is not disclosed.

filter.description: Selection, as pairs of field and value: `query` - the search string (required), `collectionId` - the collection to search in. Example: [["query", "release notes"], ["collectionId", 123]].

query.description: The search string as a parameter of its own. Superseded by filter.query and kept only so integrations do not break mid-migration; the filter wins when both are given. Move to the filter before this parameter is removed.

limit.description: Results per page, capped at 200. Defaults to 50.

offset.description: How many of the best matches to skip before the page starts. Defaults to 0; the next page is this offset plus the limit. Refused past 10000 rather than silently cut.

select.description: Fields of the result item to return. Omit for all of them.

hasMore.description: True when the answer was cut by the limit: there are matches past this page. Ask for the next one - the same limit, the offset moved on by it.

post.description:
Searches the content and titles of the documents the caller may read.

The page is chosen by an offset into the ranking: `pagination.limit` says how long the page
is (at most 200), `pagination.offset` says how many of the better matches to skip.
So the whole answer is walkable - a match past the first 200 is asked for by offset
rather than being out of reach - up to an offset of 10000, past which the request is
refused: that deep the question is the thing to narrow, not the page.

What is invisible in the listings is not found here either: search and lists are built on
one and the same visibility rule, so a document of a foreign collection exists, is indexed,
and stays out of the answer. A collection named in the filter that the caller may not open
is answered with an empty list rather than a refusal - for the same reason.

`sharedAccess` marks a hit the caller reaches through a grant on the document itself rather
than through the collection: the document is readable, the collection around it is not.

A search string shorter than 3 characters is refused: the index is built on tokens
of at least that length, so a shorter string would silently match nothing.

collectionId.description: The collection whose tree is read. A collection the caller may not open is answered as a missing one.

post.description:
Returns the documents of one collection nested into a tree, in one answer.

The answer is whole or it is a refusal: a collection holding more than
5000 documents is answered with NOTE_TREE_TOO_LARGE rather than with a part of
itself, because a caller cannot tell which branches a cut tree is missing.

The tree carries the living documents only: the main document of the collection, the
archived ones and everything in the recycle bin are left out of it. Use note.document.get
to read any of those by id - it answers for archived and trashed documents too, and reports
what they are in `isArchived` / `isTrashed` / `isOrphan`.

This method is about the shape of one collection. To find a document across collections by
its text, use note.document.search.list instead.

filter.description: Narrows the list. `state` accepts `=` and `in`; omitted, it answers with the live collections alone. `trashed` answers only with the collections the caller disposes of in the recycle bin - the right to moderate them.

pagination.description: Page of the list. Omit entirely to read the first page.

limit.description: Collections per page, capped at 200. Defaults to 50.

afterCursor.description: The nextCursor of the previous answer, passed back verbatim. Both fields are required together.

select.description: Fields to return. Omit for all of them. Narrowing the selection also skips the reads behind the fields left out, so it is worth doing on long lists.

nextCursor.description: Null on the last page. Otherwise pass it back as pagination.afterCursor.

post.description:
Lists the collections the caller may open, newest position first, page by page.

Invisible collections are absent rather than refused, so an empty list is a normal answer
and never means "no rights to use the method". Archived collections and the ones lying in
the recycle bin are left out as well, until `filter.state` asks for them by name.

Two fields say what the caller is looking at: `policyLevel` tells whether the collection is
open to the whole portal (`portal`) or only to the people named in its access rows
(`private`), and `accessLevel` tells what this particular caller may do with it
(`none` | `view` | `edit` | `full`). `accessLevel` is about the collection alone - a single
document inside it may be granted separately and higher.

Reads a single collection, archived and deleted ones included: a collection in the recycle bin answers with `state: trashed` to whoever may dispose of it there - the right to moderate it - and as a missing one to everybody else, the same way a collection the caller may not open is answered, so that its very existence is not disclosed. `markdownDescription` carries the text of the collection's main document - the description shown at the top of its knowledge base.

Creates a collection whose sole moderator is the caller: nobody else sees it until its access is given away, which REST does not do yet. Requires the portal-wide right to create collections; without it the answer is a refusal rather than an empty result.

Renames a collection. The name is the only editable field: position, access and archive state are moved by their own methods. An archived collection is read-only, and so is one in the recycle bin, so a write into either is refused - read it and show the caller why.

post.summary: Change where a collection sits in the list
post.description: Moves the collection to another place in the list of collections. The order is one for the whole portal - the same order every person sees in the sidebar - so this changes it for everybody, and it takes the portal-wide right to create collections, exactly as the sidebar does. `position` is the sort weight the listings answer with: pass a number between the weights of two collections to land between them, and omit it to land last. The weight actually stored is recomputed from the neighbours - it may differ from the one asked for - so the answer carries the collection as it was saved. An archived collection is not reordered, nor is one in the recycle bin: both are out of the list to begin with.

post.summary: Send a collection to the archive
post.description: Archives the collection together with everything inside it. An archived collection still answers reads and still comes back from note.collection.get; what it refuses is every write, and it drops out of note.collection.list. A collection that is already in the archive is answered as missing, the same refusal an already archived document gets: the archive is a state to enter, not a flag to set again. A collection in the recycle bin is not archived at all - it has to be restored first. Requires the right to moderate the collection.

post.summary: Bring a collection back from the archive
post.description: Takes the collection out of the archive with everything inside it, and it appears in note.collection.list again. A collection that is not in the archive is answered as missing, the mirror of what archiving an already archived one answers: the archive is a state to enter and to leave, not a flag to set and clear. A collection lying in the recycle bin is not unarchived either - out of the bin it would still be out of reach, so the way back is note.collection.restore first. Requires the right to moderate the collection.

post.summary: Move a collection to the recycle bin
post.description: Moves the collection to the recycle bin together with everything inside it, its description and its access list - nothing is erased, so this is not a way to destroy the content. A collection in the bin keeps answering note.collection.get with `state: trashed` for whoever may moderate it; restoring it and removing it for good are actions of the web interface. Deleting the same collection twice is not an error: the second call answers with the state the caller asked for. An archived collection may be deleted too, so an archive cannot turn into rubbish nobody is able to remove. A collection in the middle of an import is refused until the import ends. Requires the right to moderate the collection.

post.summary: Bring a collection back from the recycle bin
post.description: Takes the collection out of the recycle bin with the tree it had when it was deleted - the documents that went there with it come back where they were, and the ones thrown away earlier stay in the bin. A collection that is already out of the bin is answered with the state the caller asked for rather than with an error, so a repeated call is safe. Three refusals have codes of their own, because they are not the same news: `COLLECTION_RESTORE_IN_PROGRESS` means another restore of this collection is running and the call is worth repeating, while `COLLECTION_RETENTION_EXPIRED` (the bin has kept it longer than the retention allows) and `COLLECTION_PURGE_STARTED` (its destruction for good has begun) mean the collection is not coming back at all. Requires the right to moderate the collection - the same right that lets the caller see it in the bin in the first place.

filter.description: Narrows the list. `collectionId` keeps one knowledge base, and `0` keeps the documents that have no knowledge base at all - the ones whose base was deleted for good while they lay in the recycle bin. `state` accepts `=` and `in`; omitted, it answers with the live documents alone.

pagination.description: Page of the list. Omit entirely to read the first page.

limit.description: Documents per page, capped at 200. Defaults to 50.

afterCursor.description: The nextCursor of the previous answer, passed back exactly as it arrived. Its fields are internal and may change; a cursor that was not issued by this method is refused.

select.description: Fields to return, narrowing the answer. Omit for all of them - which is the metainformation of a document and nothing else. `markdown` is not one of them and naming it here is refused with 400: the text of a document is answered when that document is read, so ask note.document.get for it.

nextCursor.description: Null on the last page, and the only thing that says the walk is over: an answer whose items are empty while this is not null is a normal one and means "nothing on this stretch, carry on from here". Otherwise pass it back as pagination.afterCursor, unchanged.

post.description:
Lists every document the caller may read, page by page, across all their knowledge bases -
including the documents granted to them one by one inside bases they cannot otherwise open.

Invisible documents are absent rather than refused, so an empty list is a normal answer and
never means "no rights to use the method". A `collectionId` naming a base the caller may not
open is answered as a missing entity, the same way note.collection.get answers about it.

Without a `state` in the filter the answer holds the live documents alone, which is what a
client that knows nothing about archives and recycle bins expects. Ask for more by name:
`state` with `in` takes several at once. A trashed document of a base that is itself in the
recycle bin is answered only to whoever may moderate that base.

Pages are walked by cursor and not by offset: read the first page without `pagination`,
then pass the `nextCursor` of every answer back as `pagination.afterCursor` until it comes
back null. A null cursor is the only end of the walk: an answer may hold an empty `items`
while its `nextCursor` is set, and it means "nothing on this stretch, carry on from here"
rather than "no more documents" - the page is assembled from several streams of visibility
and a call reads only so far, so a long run of documents the caller cannot see can use that
up before a single row of the page is found. A loop that stops on an empty page loses
everything behind it. The cursor is opaque - store it and return it as it arrived, and do
not build one by hand. The order the documents come in is an internal matter as well: what the method
promises is that a walk started and finished with these cursors names every visible document
once, not that a particular document comes before another. A document deleted between two
pages simply stops being named.

The answer is metainformation and not content: a page holds what a client needs to show a
list and decide what to open - identifiers, title, state, dates, author, base - and not the
text of the documents. That is a rule of the module rather than a default of this method:
the text of a document is answered when that document is read, and `markdown` is refused
with 400 when a `select` names it here. A page of two hundred texts is hundreds of
megabytes, and a promise of that size is kept as a timeout or a truncated body rather than
as an answer. Read the text one document at a time with note.document.get.

This method is about which documents exist. For the shape of one base - what is nested under
what - use note.document.tree.list, and to find a document by its text, note.document.search.list.

id.description: Id of the document. One the caller may not read is answered as a missing one.

select.description: Fields to return. Omit for all of them, `markdown` included. A selection without `markdown` skips building the text altogether, which is the one expensive part of the answer.

item.title: Release notes
item.markdown:
# Release notes

The notes of the last sprint.

post.summary: One document with its text and its state
post.description:
Reads a single document: its record, its markdown, and what state it is in.

Archived and trashed documents answer here as well - they are readable, only writes into
them are refused. Which one the caller is holding is said by `state`: `live`, `archived`
or `trashed`. The markers `isArchived`, `isTrashed` and `isOrphan` say the same thing the
harder way and are deprecated - `isOrphan` means a `trashed` document whose collection is
gone, so restoring it needs a new collection to restore into.

`updatedAt` moves on a structural change of the record - a rename, a move, an archive, an
overwrite through REST. An edit in the collaborative editor deliberately moves
`contentUpdatedAt` instead, so a client watching for text changes should watch that field.

`markdown` is not the live document: it is a projection built from the editor's own format,
and `contentUpdatedAt` is the moment that projection was built, not the moment somebody last
typed. A `null` there means the projection has never been built and the markdown is empty
for that reason alone. For an archived or a trashed document the moment is final - nothing
is going to rebuild it.

The text is markdown, and it comes escaped: outside code blocks and code spans the
characters `\` `` ` `` `*` `_` `[` `]` `~` carry a backslash in front of them, and inside
a table cell the vertical bar does as well. A caller that shows the field to a human is
expected to parse it as markdown; one that matches it against plain text should drop those
backslashes first, or `some\_var\_name` will not match `some_var_name`.

The main document of a collection is not addressable here: its text is the collection's own
description, and it is read as `markdownDescription` of note.collection.get.

Creates a document in a collection, optionally under a parent document. The text is passed as markdown and is stored as the document content right away, so the fresh document reads back exactly as it was written. Requires the right to create documents in that collection.

post.summary: Rename a document or overwrite its text
post.description: Changes the title, the markdown, or both - at least one of them must be given. Overwriting the text replaces the whole document, so it is refused while somebody is editing it in the collaborative editor and their changes are not yet saved: the answer says so instead of quietly winning the race. The main document of a collection is not editable here. The markdown accepted here is capped at 1 MiB; the editor itself is not, so a document that has grown past that in the editor cannot be overwritten through REST at all - the whole text has to fit in one request.

post.summary: Send a document to the archive
post.description: Archives the document with everything nested under it. An archived document leaves the tree but is still readable through note.document.get, where it reports itself as `isArchived`. Requires the right to edit the collection it belongs to.

post.summary: Bring a document back from the archive
post.description: Takes the document and everything nested under it out of the archive and back into the tree. An archived collection around it is lifted out of the archive too - a document returned into one would be invisible anyway. A document that is not in the archive is answered as missing, the mirror of what archiving an already archived one answers: the archive is a state to enter and to leave, not a flag to set and clear. A document in the recycle bin is not in the archive - it is restored with note.document.restore. Requires the right to edit the collection it belongs to.

post.summary: Move a document, or change where it sits among its neighbours
post.description: Moves the document with everything nested under it: to another collection, under another parent, to another place in the list of its neighbours, or all three at once. The request describes where the document lands, not what changes about it - an absent `collectionId` means the collection it is in now, an absent `parentId` means a root of the target collection, so a reorder among children names its parent too. `position` is the sort weight the listings answer with: pass a number between the weights of two neighbours to land between them, and omit it to land last. The weight actually stored is recomputed from the neighbours - it may differ from the one asked for - so the answer carries the document as it was saved. Requires the right to edit both the collection the document leaves and the one it enters. A move into a branch shared with a wider audience is refused separately, as `NOTE_MOVE_ACCESS_ESCALATION`: it would hand that audience everything being moved.

post.summary: Move a document to the recycle bin
post.description: Moves the document and everything nested under it to the recycle bin, from where the web interface can still restore it - this is not a hard delete. A trashed document keeps answering note.document.get and reports itself as `isTrashed`. The main document of a collection cannot be deleted separately: it dies with the collection.

post.summary: Bring a document back from the recycle bin
post.description: Takes the document and everything nested under it out of the recycle bin. It returns to the collection it was deleted from, under its original parent whenever that parent is back in place; `collectionId` sends it elsewhere and takes the right to edit that collection. A document whose collection is gone has nowhere to return to and is refused as `NOTE_RESTORE_TARGET_REQUIRED` until `collectionId` names one. A document that is not in the bin is answered as missing, and one whose collection is in the bin is refused: the collection comes back whole, so a document pulled out of it now would be missing from it.

post.summary: Attach a file to a document
post.description: Uploads a file and links it to a document. The content is passed as base64. The answer carries `assetMarkdown` - the fragment to paste into the document text so that the file shows up in it; an image becomes a picture, anything else becomes a link. Attaching is a write on the document, so an archived or trashed one is out of reach.

post.summary: One attached file by its id
post.description: Reads the record of a file attached to a document: its name, size, type and the markdown fragment that embeds it. The binary itself is not returned. Both the file id and the document it hangs on are required - a file that belongs to another document is answered as a missing one.

documentId.description: The document whose attachments to list.

pagination.description: Page of the list. Omit entirely to read the first page.

limit.description: Attachments per page, capped at 200. Defaults to 50.

afterCursor.description: The nextCursor of the previous answer, passed back exactly as it arrived. Its fields are internal and may change; a cursor that was not issued by this method is refused.

nextCursor.description: Null on the last page. Otherwise pass it back as pagination.afterCursor, unchanged.

post.description:
Lists the files attached to a document: the same record note.file.get answers with, plus
`createdAt` - the moment the file was attached.

That date is the one the background cleanup goes by. A file uploaded through
note.file.add and never pasted into the text of the document is swept away once it is old
enough, so `createdAt` is what tells a client how long an attachment it has not used yet
still has.

Whether a file is actually pasted into the text is deliberately not reported: the text of
the document comes with note.document.get, and the client that needs to know can look for
the `assetMarkdown` of the file in it.

Listing follows the document rather than the right to write it. An archived or trashed
document the caller may still open names its attachments the same way a live one does,
and a document the caller may not see is answered as a missing entity - the same answer a
made up identifier gets.

Pages are walked by cursor and not by offset: read the first page without `pagination`,
then pass the `nextCursor` of every answer back as `pagination.afterCursor` until it
comes back null. The cursor is opaque - store it and return it as it arrived, and do not
build one by hand.

post.description:
Replaces all existing access codes for the application with the provided ones.
		For personal applications, the owner user access code is always added to the saved access codes.
		Access codes define which users or groups can use the application.
		Administrators and personal application owners always have access regardless of access codes.
		For shared applications, if no access codes are set, the application is available to everyone.
		For personal applications, if no access codes are set, only the owner and administrators have access.
		Request example:
		{
			"clientId": "local.69b9196bdbd793.03286491",
			"codes": ["UA", "D1"]
		}

Removes specified access codes from the application.
		Only the provided codes are removed; other existing codes remain unchanged.
		Administrators and personal application owners always have access regardless of access codes.
		Request example:
		{
			"clientId": "local.69b9196bdbd793.03286491",
			"codes": ["D1"]
		}

post.summary: Сбрасывает доступ приложения к значениям по умолчанию
post.description:
Removes all custom access codes and restores the default access settings for the application.
		For personal applications, the default is the owner and administrators only.
		For shared applications, the default is no restrictions (available to everyone).
		Request example:
		{
			"clientId": "local.69b9196bdbd793.03286491"
		}

Returns the current access codes assigned to the application,
		including detailed information about each code (provider and display name).
		Administrators and personal application owners always have access regardless of access codes.
		For shared applications, if no access codes are set, the application is available to everyone.
		For personal applications, if no access codes are set, only the owner and administrators have access.
		Request example:
		{
			"clientId": "local.69b9196bdbd793.03286491"

post.description:
If `handler` is provided, only the embedding with that handler will be deleted.
		If `userId` is provided, only the embedding for that user will be deleted.
		Request example:
		{
			"clientId": "local.69b9196bdbd793.03286491",
			"placement":"IM_CONTEXT_MENU"
		}

If `scope` is provided, only placements for that scope are returned, and other parameters are ignored.
		If `showAll` is `true`, all available placements are returned.
		If `clientId` is provided, only placements available to that application are returned.
		If no parameters are provided, all available placements are returned.
		Request example:
		{
			"clientId": "local.69b9196bdbd793.03286491"
		}

name.title: name
name.description: Name of the template. An absent name is inherited; a blank one is refused.

description.title: description
description.description: Description of the template in the BBCode of its editor. Comes only when the template is read back: getting it or adding a draft. An absent description is inherited, an empty one deletes it.

draftId.title: draftId
draftId.description: Draft of the current user. Comes only when the template is read back: getting it or adding a draft.

draftFingerprint.title: draftFingerprint
draftFingerprint.description: Fingerprint of the content of that draft, to be passed back to template.publish. Comes alongside draftId and is null when there is no draft. Changes whenever the draft is rewritten, which is what lets a publication refuse a graph that is no longer the one it was shown.

blocks.title: blocks
blocks.description: Blocks of the graph. Comes only when the template is read back; on write it carries the new graph.

connections.title: connections
connections.description: Connections of the graph. Comes only when the template is read back; on write it carries the graph.

returnProperties.title: returnProperties
returnProperties.description: Output properties of the block. Read-only: comes when the template is read back, and sending it refuses the request.

templateId.title: templateId
templateId.description: Template the token is bound to - the brief describes this template only.

instruction.title: instruction
instruction.description: Markdown brief for an external agent.

valid.title: valid
valid.description: The submitted graph passed both the domain validation and the post-layout check. True exactly when issues is empty; warnings do not affect it.

issues.title: issues
issues.description: Blocking problems found in the submitted graph. Empty when the graph is valid.

warnings.title: warnings
warnings.description: Non-blocking risks of the submitted graph: the graph is accepted, and the write path takes it as it is. They come with the dry run alone - a refused write answers with its problems only.

path.title: path
path.description: Full address of the problem in the submitted graph, e.g. "blocks.3.settings.1.name". Empty when the problem has no address.

blockId.title: blockId
blockId.description: Block of the submitted graph the problem belongs to. Null when the problem is not bound to a block.

code.title: code
code.description: Machine readable code of the domain error class. Null when no class is extracted for the message.

details.title: details
details.description: Server-side dictionaries explaining the problem: allowedKeys, requiredKeys, allowedOutputs, constraint, maxBytes, actualBytes, recommendedSelect. Null when the problem carries none.

hasSettings.title: hasSettings
hasSettings.description: Whether the block has an editable settings schema. Comes only in the catalog listing.

settings.title: settings
settings.description: Settings schema of the block. Comes only when a single block is read.

carriedSettings.title: carriedSettings
carriedSettings.description: Setting names whose value may only be carried over from the published template. Comes only when a single block is read.

settingConstraints.title: settingConstraints
settingConstraints.description: Cross-setting rules of the block. Comes only when a single block is read.

returnFields.title: returnFields
returnFields.description: Output properties of the block. Comes only when a single block is read.

typesDescription.title: typesDescription
typesDescription.description: Descriptions of the setting types the block uses. Comes only when a single block is read.

defaultValues.title: defaultValues
defaultValues.description: Property values the preset applies. Comes only when a single block is read, and only for a preset.

defaultSettings.title: defaultSettings
defaultSettings.description: Node topology of the block: width, height and ports. Comes only when a single block is read.

complexActions.title: complexActions
complexActions.description: Sub-action dictionary of a complex block. Comes only when a single complex block is read.

options.title: options
options.description: Value list of the field. Comes only for a field that has one.

connected.title: connected
connected.description: Whether an active session exists for this template and user.

expiresAt.title: expiresAt
expiresAt.description: Unix time the session expires at, or null when there is no session.

baseUrl.title: baseUrl
baseUrl.description: Base URL to address the contour with. Returned only when the session has just been opened; a read never carries it.

callType.title: callType
callType.description: Call type: 1 = instant ad-hoc, 2 = permanent conference room, 3 = large room.

chatId.title: chatId
chatId.description: Id of the chat the call belongs to. Opt-in: list this in `select` to receive it.

initiatorId.title: initiatorId
initiatorId.description: User id of who initiated the call.

startDate.title: startDate
startDate.description: ISO 8601 UTC timestamp when the call started.

endDate.title: endDate
endDate.description: ISO 8601 UTC timestamp when the call ended. Null while the call is still in progress.

durationSeconds.title: durationSeconds
durationSeconds.description: Total call duration in seconds (endDate − startDate).

uuid.title: uuid
uuid.description: Opaque UUID of the call session. Opt-in: list this in `select` to receive it.

language.title: language
language.description: Detected transcription language (BCP-47 / ISO 639-1, e.g. "ru", "en"). Null when there is no transcription.

version.title: version
version.description: Maximum schema version across all stored outcome blocks (transcription, overview, summary, insights, evaluation).

participants.title: participants
participants.description: Call participants, enriched with display data from Util::getUsers (name, avatar, work position). Opt-in via `select`.

outcomes.title: outcomes
outcomes.description: Names of outcome blocks present for this call: any subset of [transcription, overview, summary, insights, evaluation].

createdAt.title: createdAt
createdAt.description: ISO 8601 UTC timestamp of the most recently stored outcome record for this call.

tracks.title: tracks
tracks.description: Call recordings / tracks with download URLs. Opt-in via `select`.

transcription.title: transcription
transcription.description: Time-ordered transcription of the call with per-segment speaker attribution.

overview.title: overview
overview.description: AI overview of the meeting: topic, agenda, agreements, action items, takeaways.

summary.title: summary
summary.description: Segmented summary of the call by topic chunks.

insights.title: insights
insights.description: AI insights: per-speaker analysis with region-gated evaluation, meeting strengths/weaknesses, recommendations.

evaluation.title: evaluation
evaluation.description: Meeting efficiency evaluation: overall score and individual evaluation criteria.

language.title: language
language.description: Detected transcription language as BCP-47 / ISO 639-1 code (e.g. "ru", "en"). Null when the language could not be determined.

segments.title: segments
segments.description: Time-ordered transcription segments. Each segment is one continuous utterance by a single speaker.

topic.title: topic
topic.description: AI-detected meeting topic in one short phrase.

detailedTakeaways.description: Long-form summary of meeting outcomes (multiple sentences). @-mentions are rendered in the selected mentionFormat.

agenda.title: agenda
agenda.description: Agenda detection. Shape: { explanation: string (was an agenda announced and how it was set), quote: string (verbatim agenda quote from transcription) }.

agreements.title: agreements
agreements.description: List of explicit agreements. Each item: { agreement: string (AI-rephrased agreement, may contain @-mentions in selected mentionFormat), quote?: string (supporting transcription excerpt) }.

actionItems.title: actionItems
actionItems.description: Action items. Each item: { actionItem: string (with @-mentions), actionItemMentionLess?: string (same text without markup), quote?: string }.

meetings.title: meetings
meetings.description: Planned follow-up meetings. Each item: { meeting: string (with @-mentions), meetingMentionLess?: string, quote?: string }.

segments.title: segments
segments.description: Time-ordered segments of the meeting summary. Each segment covers a continuous topical chunk of the call.

speakerEvaluationAvailable.title: speakerEvaluationAvailable
speakerEvaluationAvailable.description: Whether per-speaker evaluation is available on this portal, gated by the license region. When false, speakerAnalysis carries no data — null in the full response shape, absent where nulls are compacted; the rest of the insights is unaffected.

speakerAnalysis.title: speakerAnalysis
speakerAnalysis.description: Per-speaker analysis, filled only when speakerEvaluationAvailable is true; when it is false the field carries no data — null where the response keeps the full shape (get, or insights / insights.speakerAnalysis in select) and absent where nulls are compacted. Each item: { userId, detailedInsight, efficiencyValue (0..100), evaluationCriteria (map of criterion->{value,criteria,title}), talkPercentage, duration (seconds), durationFormat (localized human label) }, limited to speakers matched to portal users and sorted by talkPercentage DESC, efficiencyValue DESC.

meetingStrengths.title: meetingStrengths
meetingStrengths.description: Meeting strengths. Each item: { strengthTitle: string (short label), strengthExplanation: string (detailed reasoning) }.

meetingWeaknesses.title: meetingWeaknesses
meetingWeaknesses.description: Meeting weaknesses. Each item: { weaknessTitle: string, weaknessExplanation: string }.

speechStyleInfluence.title: speechStyleInfluence
speechStyleInfluence.description: AI commentary on how speakers' communication style affected the meeting outcome.

engagementLevel.title: engagementLevel
engagementLevel.description: Free-form AI assessment of overall meeting engagement.

areasOfResponsibility.title: areasOfResponsibility
areasOfResponsibility.description: AI-detected delegated areas of responsibility and ownership coming out of the meeting.

finalRecommendations.title: finalRecommendations
finalRecommendations.description: Final AI recommendations for future meetings of this team or topic.

efficiencyValue.title: efficiencyValue
efficiencyValue.description: Overall meeting efficiency score in the range 0..100. Computed as the share of passed criteria, including the calendar overhead penalty.

calendar.title: calendar
calendar.description: Calendar booking quality. Shape: { overhead: bool } — whether the meeting ran past its scheduled end time.

criteria.title: criteria
criteria.description: Meeting evaluation criteria map. Keys are AI-driven criterion codes (e.g. agenda_clearly_stated). Each value has shape { value: bool (passed/failed), criteria: string (raw code, mirrors the key), thoughts: string (AI commentary in selected mentionFormat), title: string (localized) }.
